title: We might benefit from a "network should continue working in cases that resemble syn_cookie or syn_flood" test...
body:
### What happened?

There are kernel bugs such as https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux-hwe-5.4/+bug/1981658, which we've found on ubuntu versions, which only are visible if a node is pushed to the point that it "Switches" the way it processes packets, to the syn_cookie kernel path...

Now, Looking at https://access.redhat.com/solutions/30453, it doesnt look like we really want this to be a normal scenario...... 
```
        Note, that syncookies is fallback facility.
        It MUST NOT be used to help highly loaded servers to stand
        against legal connection rate. If you see SYN flood warnings
        in your logs, but investigation shows that they occur
        because of overload with legal connections, you should tune 
        another parameters until this warning disappear.
        See: tcp_max_syn_backlog, tcp_synack_retries, tcp_abort_on_overflow.
```

**Status**
I ran our existing e2es (iperf, networkpolicies, and sig-network tests) at high concurrency, and wasnt able to force a synflood/syncookie fallback at any point, but i know of clusters where kubelets have failed due to that path in the kernel.

**Goal**
Would be nice if we had a sig-network e2e that simulated this ?  Feel free to close if one of the existing tests already does this. 

This may or may not be possible.  I THINK that the way to do this would be to fire off lots of TCP connections.... and somehow keep them open for a long time (i.e. maybe serve very large packets?) 



### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes sig-net or similar e2e's would be able to simulate overloaded service/endpoints where non-normal TCP connection handling start happening. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not sure, thats the purpose of this test :). But... I suppose we might be able to reproduce syn-floods if theres too many TCP asks coming in at agiven time, in parallel (see above linked RH article).

title: "kubectl delete pod" doesn't kill pod's process immediately when specifying --grace-period=0
body:
### What happened?

As far as we read the help of "kubectl delete", it looks like that --grace-period=0 immediately kills Pod's processes.
```
    --force=false:
        If true, immediately remove resources from API and bypass graceful deletion. Note that immediate deletion of
        some resources may result in inconsistency or data loss and requires confirmation.

    --grace-period=-1:
        Period of time in seconds given to the resource to terminate gracefully. Ignored if negative. Set to 1 for
        immediate shutdown. Can only be set to 0 when --force is true (force deletion).
```

In fact, processes gets killed if we set --grace-period=0 in ver1.18.
But it seems that the behehavior got changed between ver1.18 and ver1.27.

- ver1.18 ... grace-period=0 killes Pod's processes immediately
- ver1.27 ... grace-period=0 sends SIGTERM to Pod's processes first, then wait for Pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds before sending SIGKILL. As a result, when I execute `kubectl delete pod grace-period=0 --force` , message "pod pod-name force deleted" is shown, but pod's process is not killed immediately. It lives during `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` .



### What did you expect to happen?

when execute "kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0" , process will have been deleted immediately unless wating during `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

nginx-pod.yaml:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.14.2
    command: [ 'sleep', '12345']
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
```

@SergeyKanzhelev Thank you. I'll test with v1.28.
Just for supplementary information; the grace period recalculation started in v1.22. Since then, the logic for changing the grace period values weren't changed until 1.28 (current released version).
is there any workaround for this?
No, There is no workaround currently.

The intended behavior here is that when the kubelet observes a pod has been force deleted, that it sends a SIGTERM to container processes as soon as it can, and then should force stop the processes with SIGKILL within 2s to give the pod an opportunity to shutdown cleanly.

Because a force deletion is the removal of a pod without waiting for clean shutdown, the kubelet handles that termination as part of its exceptional cleanup loop, which might take an extra few seconds to react.

The kubelet must never stop a container immediately with SIGKILL, and may only send that signal after attempting a SIGTERM.

EDIT: It is definitely a bug when the kubelet waits for a full termination grace period on force delete (vs the minimal wait), it’s just not immeditate in any scenario.  The bug here is waiting for the full grace period, not the fact that SIGTERM is sent.

@smarterclayton Thank you for your comments. In latest version, `SIGTERM` is sent immediately when `kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0` is executed. Because when execute `kubectl get pods` immediately after `kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0` , `No resources found in default namespace.` message is shown. But process is still living during `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default: 300). 
This behavior is different from ideal behavior that  you said " it sends a SIGTERM to container processes as soon as it can, and then should force stop the processes with SIGKILL within 2s"

title: Consume zero-sized chunked body before hijacking the connection on SPDY upgrade
body:
### What happened?

We recently faced some [some problems](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cluster-integration/gitlab-agent/-/issues/393) when using our Kube API proxy with various Kubernetes distributions. 

Long story short, the error turned out to be that in our proxy we've sent an attach request like the following to the Kube API server (simplified):

```
POST /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/tmp/attach? HTTP 1.1
Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: SPDY/3.1
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

```

The reason for this is that the go standard library writes requests with a body where it cannot determine the size as "chunked" and automatically adds the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header - so that's why the request was proxied like illustrated above.

And this is actually a problem because on the server side the handler [upgrades the connection](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f51dad586ddc1a02b4fcc4e3974092ad78b630a7/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/httpstream/spdy/upgrade.go#LL86C9-L86C9) by sending the proper `101` response and "correctly" hijacking it - however it never consumed that empty chunk (`0 CR LF CR LF`) which is still readable.
This leads to those bytes being interpreted as malformed SPDY frames.

This is clearly solvable on the client side (our proxy) - which we did.

However, it would be nice if that empty chunked data would be consumed correctly before hijacking the connection for SPDY communication.

The question here is also if the HTTP body on an upgrade request could already contain data for the upgraded protocol - the RFC is pretty vague about this, but [hints](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-upgrade:~:text=The%20capabilities%20and,to%20be%20repeated) that it's okay.

Weirdly enough this error was sporadic for us for different Kubernetes versions with different CRIs etc - so I kind of assume that some parts of the chain (maybe even only sometimes) consume that body and all works. It could also be that it works for some because one part of that chain doesn't hijack correctly - meaning they don't use the returned buffer with potentially unprocessed client data - so it may work sometimes and sometimes it doesn't - because chances are high that these `0 CR LF CR LF` end up in that buffer.

### What did you expect to happen?

A connection upgrade works even if that request contains a zero-sized chunk body.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

n/a

### Anything else we need to know?

There is a larger write up of the exact problem we've faced [here](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cluster-integration/gitlab-agent/-/issues/393).

any

nodes.title: Fix version comparison in VerifyLatestUpdate
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

We observed that version markers are not getting updated properly on many occasions which is documented in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117115

This issue appears when the version marker is supposed to switch from prerelease (rc) to stable. For example: `v1.28.0-rc.1.9+3fb5377b25ec51` -> `v1.28.0-7+c4e17abb04728e` is not going to happen even though left version is lower than right version.

The reason for that is that both `v1.28.0-rc.1.9+3fb5377b25ec51` and `v1.28.0-7+c4e17abb04728e` are considered as "prereleases" by `blang/semver` library. Version is modeled as:

| Version Part | `v1.28.0-rc.1.9+3fb5377b25ec51` | `v1.28.0-7+c4e17abb04728e` |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------  |
| Major            | 1                                                          | 1                                                     |
| Minor            | 28                                                       | 28                                                  |
| Patch            | 0                                                         | 0                                                    |
| Prerelease   | [rc, 1, 9]                                              | [7]                                                 |
| Build             | 3fb5377b25ec51                              | c4e17abb04728e                        |

Comparing versions includes comparing elements in both prerelease slices and that doesn't behave as we would expect in this case.

Given this logic, we always know that:

- Stable releases are going to have only one element in the `prerelease` slice
- Prereleases are going to have two or three elements in the `prerelease` slice

This can be used when comparing the version to properly switch from prerelease (rc) to stable.

There might be a better approach, but I didn't find such an approach from [the `blang/semver` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/blang/semver/v4). Unit tests are added to cover various cases and ensure that this still works as expected.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117115

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fix version comparison in VerifyLatestUpdate
```

cc @kubernetes/release-engineering 
/hold for discussion

What do you think of the following possible solution:
1. Create and checkpoint a `claimInfo()` with minimal information *before* calling `NodePrepareResource()`.
2. Fill the `claimInfo()` with the rest of its info and checkpoint it again *after* `NodePrepareResource()` if it succeeds.
3. Delete and checkpoint the `claimInfo()` *after* `NodePrepareResource()` if it fails.
4. When restoring the checkpoint after kubelet startup, for any empty `claimInfo()` objects, spawn off a goroutine to populate it with a call to `NodePrepareResource()`. Spin on this "forever" until it succeeds.
5. In `NodeUnprepareResources()` error out if we ever encounter an empty `claimInfo()`.

We would need to make sure we have a way to stop calling `NodePrepareResource()` in the gorouting at some point (i.e. if/when the plugin responsible for it deregisters), but I think something like this should work.

title: kubelet: Evicted and force deleted pods get their full termination grace period when they should not
body:
### What happened?

When pods are evicted, i.e. with a hard eviction, the grace period is intended to be `0s` (i.e. do not respect the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`). 

However, currently, evicted pods receive their full termination grace period seconds.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod is evicted immediately and the termination grace period is not respected 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the following pod which has an ephemeral storage limit of 5Mi and uses `dd` to fill the disk

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: evictdiskpod
  labels:
    pod: evictdiskpod
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    resources:
      limits:
        ephemeral-storage: 5Mi
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        sleep 10
        dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10
        echo 'write done'
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2. Observe the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds was respected when it should've not been

In the logs:

```
# I added a debug print to include grace period here (it is zero)
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688802     275 eviction_manager.go:583] "Evicting pod" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 message="Pod ephemeral local storage usage exceeds the total limit of containers 5Mi. " grace period=0


Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688838     275 pod_workers.go:649] "Pod is being evicted by the kubelet, begin teardown" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688937     275 pod_workers.go:906] "Processing pod event" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 updateType=1
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688965     275 pod_workers.go:1026] "Pod worker has observed request to terminate" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734

# syncTerminatingPod has a grace period of 60 (unexpected since it should've been overridden to zero)

Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.688980     275 kubelet.go:1859] "syncTerminatingPod enter" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 gracePeriod=60
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.689132     275 kubelet.go:1891] "Pod terminating with grace period" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 gracePeriod=60
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.689171     275 kuberuntime_container.go:707] "Killing container with a grace period override" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 containerName="busybox" containerID="containerd://71e017fbdc6de9cafc7aa136e2bb07c5d02891db21eacec0c6d358e46125ef1e" gracePeriod=60
Feb 16 02:13:01 kind-worker kubelet[275]: I0216 02:13:01.689193     275 kuberuntime_container.go:711] "Killing container with a grace period" pod="default/evictdiskpod" podUID=3257107a-73ff-455a-8286-74d350c6d734 containerName="busybox" containerID="containerd://71e017fbdc6de9cafc7aa136e2bb07c5d02891db21eacec0c6d358e46125ef1e" gracePeriod=60
```

Full kubelet logs: https://gist.github.com/bobbypage/7ef6335c5ee69ef8ba363d6edf5854e9


### Anything else we need to know?

1. When pod ephemeral storage eviction is reached  `evictPod` is called with a zero grace period

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L535

2. `evictPod` uses killPod and passes the zero grace period

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/eviction/eviction_manager.go#L584-L591

3. Eventually the grace period is set here in pod worker

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L694-L700

4. `calculateEffectiveGracePeriod` is used to calculate the grace period. The `options.PodTerminationGracePeriodSecondsOverride` is set to zero (which originates from the eviction manager). This overrides the pod spec's grace period here (the comment mentions this case is for eviction manager):

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/908803081fd4554d7cdb17cb77e5490c44ef7ab7/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L793-L800

5. But... the bug is that right after we check the grace period happened to be zero (`gracePeriod == 0`) and if it is we change it back pod spec's grace period, thus losing the `options.PodTerminationGracePeriodSecondsOverride`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/908803081fd4554d7cdb17cb77e5490c44ef7ab7/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L801-L805

and now the final grace period returned is the pod spec's grace period instead of the overriden grace period from the eviction manager. 





### Kubernetes version

Reproduced in 1.26.0

But in the logs, the full grace period was given:

nice catch

We definitely need to clarify the intended behavior of the various overrides.  I think it should be:

| Scenario | Expected grace period | Runs hooks | Urgent | Comments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| User deletes in API without specifying grace period | pod | Y | N | Includes invoking pod API eviction (`pods/eviction`) |
| User deletes in API without specifying grace period and pod has value 1 | minimum | Y | N | " |
| User deletes in API with delete grace period 1 | minimum | Y | N | " |
| User deletes in API with delete grace period `N` | `N` | Y | N | " |
| Pod is force deleted from API and kubelet observes delete grace period 1 | minimum | Y | Y | We should verify we have a test in API that ensures the intermediate write happens (pretty sure we do) |
| Pod is force deleted from API and kubelet does not observe the immediate write | minimum | Y | Y |
| Kubelet evicts a pod (node eviction) | minimum | Y | Y | This should probably be described as *urgent* - we want to end the process as quickly as possible to guarantee node health.  See below.  Note also a node eviction and pod API eviction are not the same - pod API eviction respects backpressure defined by a PDB user/admin intent, node eviction respects backpressure from the physical limits of a node. |
| User updates a static pod with a fixed UID | pod | Y | N |
| User deletes and then recreates a static pod with a fixed UID | pod | Y | N |
| User updates a static pod with a dynamic UID | pod | Y | N |
| Kubelet detects a soft admission exclusion for an already running pod | minimum | Y? | Maybe? | Soft admission exclusion is roughly eviction, but not quite. |
| Kubelet detects an orphaned runtime pod | minimum | N | Y | We don't know the orphaned pod's spec | 

We need to decide how best-effort hooks are. My position would likely be:

> Most hooks and most SIGTERM should exit << 1s (which is our described minimum), and the pod author is the one who designs the hook, so they are responsible for fitting within the shutdown window. So if a pod author writes a slow shutdown hook that is intentional and within their control, so we want the hook to get the bulk of the shutdown window. However, given that termination is granular to the second, the minimum duration for hooks is 1s and the minimum duration for kill is 1. Hooks are best effort, and under the presence of errors we do not guarantee that
a pre-stop hook is executed before the pod is killed, we only guarantee that we make an attempt at least once to
run a hook.

### Minimum with hooks

1. Hook is invoked with 1s minimum shutdown time, at 1s we cancel the invocation
2. Terminate containers is invoked with 1s minimum shutdown time in parallel per container (TERM, 1s, KILL)

If we encounter an error during invocation of a hook under minimum shutdown conditions, we should move immediately to terminating the containers

### Minimum without hooks

1. Terminate containers is invoked with 1s minimum shutdown time in parallel per container

### "Urgent" termination

Pod eviction is intended to reduce pressure on the node to forestall hard failure (OOM, soft-lock, livelock, etc).  We cannot perfectly predict hard failure, and cgroups v2 improves our ability to mitigate failure at a lower level in the kernel for certain classes (memory pressure).  In hard failure scenarios, processes can be terminated without recourse due to byzantine failure modes, which implies that we are allowed to be best effort at both hooks and sending TERM vs KILL.

I suggest we define "urgent" termination as:

> In order to prevent subsequent unpredictable failures, and having made reasonable effort to gracefully terminate a pod, the kubelet may bypass hooks and the transmission of a TERM signal and move straight to KILL for the pod.

An urgent termination is the system acting within the definition of "best effort" for shutdown while balancing its responsibility to other workloads.  Pods that assume that they will always receive TERM, or always get their hooks invoked, are already broken (force delete, for instance, or a hard node failure).

In practice this would mean that terminations marked urgent (need better name) will try N times to invoke hooks (if available) and N times to send TERM, and after that move to a hard termination mode where we ignore all hooks and send no TERM (if that's even possible with CRI?).  If necessary we can KEP this.

### How do we handle errors during attempts to terminate

The syncTerminatingPod method is called repeatedly until the runtime heals (returns without error), with some backoff in pod worker.  This is problematic in eviction.  We probably should consider behavior of errors past the grace period differently from errors before the grace period expires (as observed by the kubelet - i.e. if grace period is 30s after 30s we switch from "happy path" to "you're gone" path).  We might simply define urgent as "you're past the grace period" and have termination behavior keyed to that (errors in hooks are ignored?)
Node Drains also evict pods via the API. API based Evictions should probably honor the graceful termination. @smarterclayton could you add this scenario to the matrix?

An API based eviction is a delete of a pod in either of the first two scenarios, I'll add a comment.  An API based eviction isn't a "node eviction", so I'll also clarify that terminology.

Edit: updated with both distinctions.
/triage accepted

out of curiosity, can anyone tell what was the intention of this comment in L699
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L694-L700
saying that the grace period `will never be zero`

is this by design that it is never expected to be zero? should the specification be updated so that the grace-period argument does not take `0` ?

To further support my above inquiry, it appears that gracePeriod is never expected to be `0` because anything less than `1` is set to `1`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L807-L810

Which raises the question of the need for allowing `0` to be an acceptable user-specifiable gracePeriod value. Since "immediate" is considered to be equivalent to to `gracePeriod` being `1`.

> Hooks are best effort, and under the presence of errors we do not guarantee that
a pre-stop hook is executed before the pod is killed, we only guarantee that we make an attempt at least once to
run a hook.

Anecdotally, the pre-stop hook for force delete pods (and possibly, evicted pods) is being executed only as of #115835, which debuted in K8s 1.28.

Prior to that (e.g., in 1.27), the `gracePeriod` variable was being set to `0` by `setTerminationGracePeriod` (because `pod.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds` is 0 on force deletion), and thus the condition for executing the pre-stop hook isn't fullfiled:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1b4df30b3cdfeaba6024e81e559a6cd09a089d65/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L721-L731

As of #115835 (e.g., in 1.28), `gracePeriod` is overridden and hence `!= 0`, so pre-stop does execute. 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/855e7c48de7388eb330da0f8d9d2394ee818fb8d/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L722-L738

Note though, that now the full `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is applied to the hook execution, even upon force deletion.

> Note though, that now the full `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is applied to the hook execution, even upon force deletion.

I think this is what #120451 is trying to address.

> To further support my above inquiry, it appears that gracePeriod is never expected to be `0` because anything less than `1` is set to `1`.
> 
> https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a25834cb5a16bbd6a9295aeb5d1621aa8a4cd407/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L807-L810
> 
> Which raises the question of the need for allowing `0` to be an acceptable user-specifiable gracePeriod value. Since "immediate" is considered to be equivalent to to `gracePeriod` being `1`.

I'm also interested in understanding the reason for not allowing 0 grace period. This is mentioned again [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120451#discussion_r1439851789).

Intuitively, I would have thought that we would send 0 grace period to the CRI which would know how to handle it.

Related:

- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/120449

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Currently when evicting pods due to resource pressure, or when a pod's storage use has exceeded the configured ephemeral-storage resource limit, we use a grace period override of 0 during eviction which actually ends up allowing the pod's full configured grace period rather than performing an immediate eviction due to the logic [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/227c2e7c2b2c05a9c8b2885460e28e4da25cf558/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L998-L1000)

In order to actually perform an immediate eviction we should instead use a grace period override of 1 in these cases.

This is the same as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119570 but rebased. I don't mind which of these is merged, we just really need this fix.

```release-note
Fixes a bug where hard evictions due to resource pressure would let the pod have the full termination grace period, instead of shutting down instantly. This bug also affected force deleted pods. Both cases now get a termination grace period of 1 second.

title: PVC recreation needed when Stateful set Pod stuck in pending
body:
### What happened?

- User cordons a node with a pvc bound to a local persistent volume
- User deletes a stateful set pod from that node
- The pod is in pending because the pvc is still bound to a local pv on the cordoned node (expected)
- The node dies and the pvc is deleted
- The pod is still stuck in pending because the pvc is missing (bug)

The pod now needs to be manually deleted so that the pod+pvc can be recreated

### What did you expect to happen?

After the pvc was deleted, the statefulset controller should have recreated it and bound it to a new node's local pv so that the pending pod could be scheduled. Currently the only way to get the pod out of pending is to manually delete it so that it recreates itself and its pvc

We used https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/sig-storage-local-static-provisioner for the local PVs, but the problem is not limited to this particular provisioner

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- create a stateful set with a pvc that is bound to a local PV
- use `kubectl cordon` to cordon a node with a local pv
- delete a statefulset pod from that node
- delete the pvc from that node

the pod is now stuck in pending due to a missing pvc

### Anything else we need to know?

There was a related issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/74374 but this only fixed the issue when the order of operations was delete pvc -> delete pod. but in this case, it is delete pod -> delete pvc

title: [scale] node state changes causes excessive LB re-configurations
body:
### What happened?

There is scale bug related to the cloud-controller-manager, namely: when a cluster reaches a state where the relation between the amount of LBs and cluster nodes reaches an almost equal amount (i.e: a many-to-many relation between LBs and nodes) the amount of cloud API calls performed by the CCM to sync LBs can become overwhelming for the cloud provider. This can (among other things) lead to:

1. an excessive amount of cloud API calls for the LB re-configurations
2. rate limiting by the cloud provider as an effect of 1.
3. or worse: a non-trivial amount of time to sync all services in the cluster, leading to desynchronized LBs.

An example of problem 3. is: imagine we have 200 LBs and 500 nodes, on clusters at such scale, the amount of events processed by the CCM for transitioning node state can become important. The current implementation of the CCM will resync all 200 LB services for any node which has a transitioning state - as to keep the LBs' configured backends in sync with the state of the cluster. It has been observed that on clusters at that scale, the cloud provider can take up to hours to process a full resync for all services. A scenario such as the below is hence not improbable (and actually quite likely):

1. Node25 transitions from Ready -> NotReady
[All LB services are synced - time taken for this might be long]
2. Service1's LB which only has an endpoint on Node25 gets Node25 removed from its list of backend
3. Node25 transitions from NotReady -> Ready again, cancelling the scheduled eviction for the endpoint hosted on Node25 for Service1
4. CCM is still processing the updated caused by 1. and clients connecting to the LB of Service1 continues experiencing connectivity issues, even though Node25 now is in a Ready state.
[Eventually - once the CCM enters its second reconciliation loop caused by 3.]
5. The LB for Service1 gets Node25 added to its list of backend again and connectivity is again achieved by clients.

The sync function which is triggered when a node transitions state from Ready <-> NotReady, is currently correct but can be avoided for services which have ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal if the service does not have an endpoint on any of the nodes which are transitioning state between Ready <-> NotReady. This is because such services are not designed to forward traffic to any other node, and the update is thus useless to them. The node which is experiencing a transitioning state is already configured for that LB, and the fact that it transitions state is a moot point for what concerns these services. 

The longer vision I have for this: remove the sync function for transitioning node readiness state from the CCM altogether and instead have all services of type LoadBalancer evaluate the node's readiness state by the utilization of a LB configured health check probe against the [kubelet's read-only port](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cluster/ports/ports.go#L33). This would allow transitioning node readiness state to be handled much more dynamically (similar to what has already been implemented for HealthCheckNodePort by kube-proxy) for all services of type LoadBalancer irrespectively of if they define ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal or not....but that will require a enhancement proposal since cloud providers have divergent implementations of how they configure health check probes for LB services.

I am putting this here for completeness sake: this is what the major cloud providers currently do to health check services which are not ExternalTrafficPolicyLocal

GCE: probes [10256](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/cluster/ports/ports.go#L36)
AWS: if ELB: probes the first NodePort defined on the service spec.
Azure: probes all NodePort defined on the service spec.

All of these can be improved, but an enhancement proposal would be needed to align them all. For now: this PR will help fix some cases.

### What did you expect to happen?

Node readiness changes should not re-configure load balancers associated with services of type ETP=local. 

- Nodes not hosting any endpoints associated with these services do not forward traffic to nodes that do, so re-configuring the LB because said node goes NotReady is useless. 
- Nodes hosting endpoints associated with these services are already health checked using the HC probe configured for the `healthCheckNodePort` and can rely on that much more dynamically without needing to re-configure the LB. 

In the long-term: all load balancers should not be re-configured because of node state changes. That will need an enhancement proposal however (which I am currently drafting) to change service proxies and align cloud provider HCs. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

"as minimally and precisely as possible" not sure if this hits the definition, but: we need a big cluster with a lot of entropy (for example by performing an upgrade and restarting all nodes one-by-one) - this should end up re-configuring every single LB N*M (where N is the amount of nodes and M is the amount of state transitions per node). 

### Anything else we need to know?

All versions.


### Cloud provider

All cloud providers.

$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a

C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

/sig network 
/sig cloud-provider

I am doubtful I should open a new issue for this (seeing as how it's very much correlated to this issue), but there's another problem exherbitated by re-configuring the LB when not really needed; 

Updating a service from `ExternalTrafficPolicy = Cluster` to `ExternalTrafficPolicy = Local` can/will cause minute-wide blackouts for the service SLAs.

Specifically, when such an update is issued on the service object: kube-proxy will update all rules on nodes not hosting any endpoint and stop traffic from being forwarded, this is "the fast path". Inefficiently however, the CCM will also trigger a re-configuration of the LBs HC, which is the "slow path". Any client attempting to connect to the application backed by this service will not be able to until the LB is fully re-configured, since the LB won't have an HC or an incomplete one not being able to fully indicate where traffic should be sent. It feels ridiculous that such a small change can lead to such high windows of observed downtime - this is particularly impactful on low latency applications with strict SLAs.  

This can't be fixed today without that enhancement proposal, but I think that in an ideal world (hopefully once the KEP is in) the HC for what concerns the LB should remain the same. The only real change should, on such an update, be the service proxy's response to that HC. That would severely reduce the observed "downtime". That obviously means impacting the `healthCheckNodePort`, since that port will need to be aligned with the default HC port for ETP!=Local services. At the same time users can specify what that port should be, so maybe the default port should change if the service has a `healthCheckNodePort` already defined? Te be discussed on the KEP...

title: Cannot use hostAliases when mounting files in /etc
body:
### What happened?

I have a file that I mount in /etc and if I use hostAliases feature then pod goes into RunContainerError state.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the pod to be deployed without errors.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Here is a sample config that causes this condition:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: v1
data:
  nsswitch.conf: |
    hosts: files dns
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nss
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: web
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: web
    volumeMounts:
    - name: nss
      mountPath: /etc
  volumes:
  - name: nss
    configMap:
      name: nss
      items:
      - key: nsswitch.conf
        path: nsswitch.conf
  hostAliases:
  - hostnames:
    - kubernetes
    ip: 10.0.0.1
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always
---
```

@surajssd 
> I have a file that I mount in /etc and if I use hostAliases feature then pod goes into RunContainerError state.

The problem here is not with hostAliases as far as I can see. You use /etc as a mount point for the config map. This creates a **read-only** volume mounted on /etc, which makes it impossible for OCI runtime to mount resolv.conf there:

rootfs_linux.go:76: mounting "/var/lib/docker/containers/160ad34a2ab1ed1288fa3037041f03ce89992b84d9363838df051de454398892/resolv.conf" to rootfs at "/etc/resolv.conf" caused: open /var/lib/docker/overlay2/fdbff16e45635a8a837b48ad757100e47cb3d34b2428a0c81e097e9262a9ad9d/merged/etc/resolv.conf: **read-only** file system: unknown

I don't think this is a proper usage of configMap. However, you can use `subpath` as suggested above. Here is a working configuration:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
data:
  hosts: files dns
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nss
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: web
    volumeMounts:
    - name: nss
      mountPath: /etc/nsswitch.conf
      subPath: hosts
  volumes:

    configMap:
      name: nss
  hostAliases:
  - hostnames:
    - kubernetes
    ip: 10.0.0.1
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always

```

title: `kubectl get <resource>.<group>` invalidates discovery
body:
**What happened**:

Ran the following on a cluster with many custom resources installed:

```
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | \
  xargs -n 1 kubectl get --show-kind --ignore-not-found -n my-namespace
```

The command took longer to run than expected. Adding trace logging with `--v=6`, the `kubectl get` call was invalidating discovery data on every invocation, meaning every `kubectl get` call fully re-fetched discovery data.

This can be reproduced by making a `kubectl get` call with a single `<resource>.<group>` argument as output by `api-resources -o name`:

```
... install a CRD that defines a `foos` resource in the `example.com` API group ...

# fetch to ensure discovery data including the new custom resource is cached
kubectl get foos.example.com

# refetch and observe discovery data is invalidated
kubectl get foos.example.com --v=6
I1109 15:06:06.874348   74544 loader.go:375] Config loaded from file:  /Users/liggitt/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/certs/admin.kubeconfig
I1109 15:06:06.879882   74544 discovery.go:214] Invalidating discovery information
I1109 15:06:06.889069   74544 round_trippers.go:444] GET https://localhost:6443/api?timeout=32s 200 OK in 9 milliseconds
I1109 15:06:06.912802   74544 round_trippers.go:444] GET https://localhost:6443/apis?timeout=32s 200 OK in 1 milliseconds
I1109 15:06:06.939306   74544 round_trippers.go:444] GET https://localhost:6443/apis/certificates.k8s.io/v1beta1?timeout=32s 200 OK in 2 milliseconds
I1109 15:06:06.940452   74544 round_trippers.go:444] GET https://localhost:6443/apis/authorization.k8s.io/v1?timeout=32s 200 OK in 3 milliseconds
...
```

**What you expected to happen**:

Cached discovery data to be used

nodes.body: /sig api-machinery cli

The reason seems to be we falsely parse, for example, `endpointslice.discovery.k8s.io` to `k8s.io/discovery, Resource=endpointslice`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/307278029cbf69bc35a7795594d970b7781de2b8/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema/group_version.go#L29-L37

So the match failed, `err != nil` is true, triggered reset here.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/307278029cbf69bc35a7795594d970b7781de2b8/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/restmapper/discovery.go#L230-L233

But the retry failed, too.

Then the logic of `fullySpecifiedGVR != nil` failed, falls to the second if, which uses `groupResource` :

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/307278029cbf69bc35a7795594d970b7781de2b8/staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource/builder.go#L716-L731


![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14567045/98931711-55deb180-2519-11eb-90c8-f960855627a5.png)

Note that the second param is `endpointslice.v1beta1.discovery.k8s.io`.


We could change the parse function per [the doc](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/#api-versioning) to fix this issue. I will create a PR later.

> We could change the parse function per [the doc](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/#api-versioning) to fix this issue.

I think the parse function is doing the right thing ... both the `<resource>.<group>` and `<resource>.<version>.<group>` forms are allowed, and the parse function returns both.

The code that uses those return values to locate a resource is triggering cache invalidation when the first check fails. The rest mapper interface doesn't have a "KindForButDoNotInvalidateIfNotFound" method, which is what we really want when we're calling from mappingFor (we want to see if fullySpecifiedGVR or groupResource.WithVersion("") resolve, and only if neither do, then invalidate
I think we shouldn't keep a wrong parsed result if we can make it right.

> I think we shouldn't keep a wrong parsed result if we can make it right.

it's not wrong. there are two supported ways to parse a.b.c, and we have to try both:

* resource=a, group=b.c
* resource=a, version=b, group=c
I know this. But in this situation (`endpointslice.discovery.k8s.io`), it treats `discovery` as version.
Why we have to call KindFor twice if we could done the task once?

because we don't know whether `a.b.c.d` represents `resource=a, version=b, group=c.d` or `resource=a, group=b.c.d`, and calling `KindFor` is currently how we determine which is correct.

Resolving this will likely require a new signature or mechanism for interrogating the restmapper

We already have a [version definition](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/#api-versioning).

> Alpha: The version names contain alpha (for example, v1alpha1).
Beta: The version names contain beta (for example, v2beta3).
Stable: The version name is vX where X is an integer.

that's a convention (followed by all the APIs shipped by the Kubernetes project), but is not guaranteed for custom/aggregated resources:

```
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: weirds.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: mylevel1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
  - name: mylevel2
    served: true
    storage: false
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
  names:
    singular: weird
    plural: weirds
    kind: Weird
    listKind: WeirdList
---
kind: Weird
apiVersion: example.com/mylevel1
metadata:
  name: test
```

```
kubectl get weirds.mylevel1.example.com
NAME   AGE
test   15s
```

if the a.b.c.d matches a group, version, and kind, we should prefer that since it is fully qualified

Could you provide advice on how to resolve this?
IMO I will add a pair enable/disable function to `CachedDiscoveryInterface` to control how function `Fresh` works, instead of adding a `KindForButDoNotInvalidateIfNotFound` because we may need many `XXXButNotInvalidation` functions further, and not every rest mapper has a cache behavior.

We could introduce an `Option` function to rest mapper interface to control its behavior (although I don't know what behavior we want to control further except this situation).
/triage accepted
I'm not sure off the top of my head... @deads2k might have some advice

> I'm not sure off the top of my head... @deads2k might have some advice

We added etags to open-api, what if we did similar to discovery to inform the caching?  Do etags allow us arbitrarily set a different etag even when content has not changed?  If we could do that, then we could have a discovery rule that says etags are updated whenever a "lower" discovery doc changes.  So a version discovery change (adding a resource) would ripple out to update etags for the group, and for the list of apis.  This would allow a clever REST mapper to only traverse requests as far the last change to discovery.  If nothing changed, then only two requests would be needed (/api and /apis).

Caveat: I'm not sure if the etag spec allows arbitrary etag changes.
Maybe related: #44957

title: kubectl apply --prune --all fails to remove existing resources
body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug

**What happened**:

I ran
```
kubectl apply --all --namespace default --prune -f base/ --recursive
```

It applied all my new yaml in base/ but did not remove existing resources from the cluster due to an error:

I believe I read in some other issue that there are (still?) some plans to improve the whole apply/prune handling. However, for this specific issue, there is some kind of workaround by using prune-whitelist.

The command from the initial description

```
kubectl apply --all --namespace default --prune -f myservice.yaml
```

could be rewritten like this:

```
kubectl apply --namespace default --prune --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/ConfigMap' \
  --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/Endpoints' --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/PersistentVolumeClaim' \
  --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/Pod' --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/ReplicationController' \
  --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/Secret' --prune-whitelist 'core/v1/Service' \
  --prune-whitelist 'batch/v1/Job' --prune-whitelist 'batch/v1beta1/CronJob' \
  --prune-whitelist 'extensions/v1beta1/DaemonSet' \
  --prune-whitelist 'extensions/v1beta1/Deployment' \
  --prune-whitelist 'extensions/v1beta1/Ingress' --prune-whitelist 'extensions/v1beta1/ReplicaSet' \
  --prune-whitelist 'apps/v1beta1/StatefulSet' --prune-whitelist 'apps/v1beta1/Deployment' \
  -f myservice.yaml
```

However, this approach has the following drawbacks:

1. I don't know if the list of objects is complete
2. When new objects are added by Kubernetes, this list needs to be updated
3. It doesn't consider custom resource definitions

So if you really need to make it work right now, I think this workaround could be OK. For the long run, hopefully the apply/prune mechanism will be improved to better handle cases like this.

title: kubelet's calculation of whether a container has changed can cause cluster-wide outages
body:
Updated 2020-11-09 by @liggitt:

In 1.16+, the kubelet hashes the serialized container spec:

1. API server sends data
    * Defaults for added fields will modify this data
    * If an alpha field that is not defaulted graduates to adding a default in beta, an API server upgrade from alpha->beta will modify this data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/apis/core/v1/defaults_test.go#L165-L167
2. Kubelet decodes that data into its v1.Container struct
    * If the kubelet is older than the API server, this means it will drop fields added in newer API server versions
3. Kubelet encodes that v1.Container struct to JSON and hashes that data
    * https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f1e5cafd33a8863c5dfe9f36c9cba836f0e981b/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L98-L108

This mechanism is used by the kubelet in `containerChanged` and `getStableKey`, which means an API server upgrade that starts defaulting a container field graduating from alpha will instantly modify the computed hash and trigger a container restart. This results in simultaneous restart of all containers across all pods of a replicaset and can cause outages.

The kubelet should limit the fields it considers in the container hash to the ones it expects to be able to change in ways that would affect the running container (currently just `image`, I think). The pod uid is already included in `getStableKey` so a delete/recreate of the entire pod would already compute a different key.

Changing this mechanism on a minor version boundary (to improve the interactions with the API server changes in 1) is acceptable, because pods are expected to be drained as part of that upgrade (xref https://github.com/kubernetes/website/issues/12326#issuecomment-704469840)


-----------

Original description:

Kubelet hashes the container spec and store it with the container so that it can detect whether the container meets the current spec. If the hashes do not match, kubelet would kill the container and create a new one. The most notable side effect of this mechanism is that if a new field is added to the container spec in the 1.x kubernetes version, and kubelet is upgraded to 1.x from 1.x-1 version, all containers created by the 1.x-1 version kubelet will be killed.

This issue has come up quiet a few time before (see #53644), and discussed extensively in #23104. It was punted a few times because 1) in-place upgrade of kubelet was not officially supported, and 2) upgrading docker used to require restarting all the containers too. Now that upgrade is managed by the installers (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/6099#issuecomment-359331190) and docker supports live-restore, we should consider fixing this in kubelet.

There are related discussions/suggestions the #57741 PR already. Creating this issue as a centralized place for discussions and suggestions.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node-feature-requests 
/cc a couple of folks who have expressed interests in this issue: @dixudx @kevin-wangzefeng @wackxu

nodes.body:
As @lavalamp suggested in #23104, instead of hash the whole container spec, can we maintain a list of container fields of different releases that should be taken into consideration during hash, and identify the hash values with release prefix?
The field list may looks like:
```
release1: {field1, field2...fieldN}
release2: {field1, field2...fieldN, fieldN+1}
```
and imagine the kubelet has been upgraded to release2 (new container field `fieldN+1`  added), when walking through the pods, if it found a container has a hash with a prefix of "release1", then it knows the container should be hashed with the fields of release1, thus, the result hash would not change.

And if the users have an update on a pod or its deployment, then the pod is expected to be recreated, thus, the fields of new release begin to take effect on its containers.

The only downside I can think of is that we might need to maintain the field list manually (e.g deprecate the field of old releases).

> can we maintain a list of container fields of different releases that should be taken into consideration during hash

That means we have to hard code this. I don't like this way.

As I mentioned in [#57741](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/57741#issuecomment-356196638), how about adding a new label, like `containerSerializedSpecLabel `, with backwards compatibility supported as well.

> As I mentioned in #57741, how about adding a new label, like `containerSerializedSpecLabel`, with backwards compatibility supported as well.

We don't have field level versioning for kubernetes api today, so it won't help (kubelet itself has no idea which version a field is introduced or changed).

If we have to go with the field label approach, adding a version indicator might help:
For example 

```go
type Container struct {
    foo string `containerSerializedSpecLabel:"since v1.9"`
    bar string `containerSerializedSpecLabel:"since v1.10"`
}
```
Then, `foo` will be included for checking container hash like "v1.9-xxxxxxxx" 
`foo` and `bar` will be included for checking container hash like "v1.10-xxxxxxxx"

TBO, I don't see many benefits than having a container fields list const some where in pkg/kubelet,(e.g. in `pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go`)

Another problem with comparing hashes across versions is changes to the hash function.

Similar issues have come up in workload controllers, where they are used for collision avoidance only, for these types of reasons. 

Persisted hashes shouldn't be used as the sole determination of equality, since there are multiple reasons why they may change across releases.

If a hash comparison fails, one needs to fall back to actually comparing properties that matter. 

cc @janetkuo @kow3ns

You can solve it with hashes, but you need to hash whitelisted fields (NOT
the encoded object), store every iteration of the hash function, and
understand a vector of hashes (i.e., one label per iteration of the hash
function) instead of a single hash.

In order to fix this issue, I suppose PR #57741 help to omit nil/empty filed from now on, even new filed was added in the future. I will prevent restarting container continues. we need to make decision to close this kind of issue since 1.8.x -> 1.9.x, 1.11.x -> 1.12.x and so on.
It does not help for migration immediately to omit nil/empty filed, but if it go into 1.16.x from now on, it will help on future upgrade from 1.16.x -> 1.17.x and so on.

Is this a proper time to re-consider this issue, find a one-time fix? 

We still struggle from container restart when trying to upgrade our 1.15.x cluster, backport #57741 won't help since itself would bring a hash change.
And #57741 can't deal with new added filed with default value(and maybe delete desperated field in the furture).  Nil default proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/community/pull/4571 may help fix this issue forever with #57741, but it seems discussion moved to another approach(use generation or server side apply), which can't apply in this situation.

`containerSerializedSpecLabel` approach @liggitt @dixudx proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/57741#issuecomment-356196638 make sense to me. Backwards compatibility can be done with serialize the current container spec and deserialize into a legacy container spec which we previously stored for compatibility. This will guarantee a smooth upgrade.

cc @thockin who may help with some input.
Changing the kubelet mechanism on a minor version boundary is acceptable, because pods are expected to be drained on kubelet minor version upgrade.

Updated the title and description to clarify the impact of the current logic and why it should be changed

xref discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/95587#issuecomment-742126350
my naive recommendation would be to limit the container hash to specific fields that are known to be immutable or are expected to be able to change (maybe just name and image?)

> limit the container hash to specific fields that are known to be immutable or are expected to be able to change

✅  💯 

If kubelet doesn't know how to react to a field change, it must not be included in the hash.

In-place upgrades add some restrictions:
* The hash must be versioned so that a future kubelet which knows how to react to additional field changes doesn't do an unnecessary restart. (it has to be able to reproduce the hashes of the old kubelet.)
* A new hash version must not be used until there's no chance of rolling back to an old kubelet version which doesn't understand it.

(the above goes for controllers that perform this operation, too)

> maybe just name and image

And resource limits, if those would require a restart.

> In-place upgrades add some restrictions:
> 
> * The hash must be versioned so that a future kubelet which knows how to react to additional field changes doesn't do an unnecessary restart. (it has to be able to reproduce the hashes of the old kubelet.)
> * A new hash version must not be used until there's no chance of rolling back to an old kubelet version which doesn't understand it.

Specifically for kubelets, if the change is made on a minor version boundary, I don't think we need those protections, given sig-node's position that in-place (minor version) kubelet upgrades without draining is not supported.

> (the above goes for controllers that perform this operation, too)

Yes, for controllers, which have to deal with persisted ControllerRevisions and annotations on API objects made by earlier versions of the controller, they definitely have to consider the approach taken by previous versions of the controller. I plan to spawn similar issues to track resolving this for controllers

> in-place kubelet upgrades without draining is not supported.

Oh, I did not know this. What is the point of in-place upgrades then?
Expanded my previous comment... in place *minor version* kubelet upgrades are not supported without draining. I think in place patch version upgrades are.

Ah, OK, I can see why you call it optional, but I think it's bad karma unless we have some system that guarantees we don't make a mistake over a patch version change. Perhaps we could resolve that with e.g. a golden data test.

> Yes, for controllers, which have to deal with persisted ControllerRevisions and annotations on API objects made by earlier versions of the controller, they definitely have to consider the approach taken by previous versions of the controller. I plan to spawn similar issues to track resolving this for controllers

Is there a particular problem that impacts the user wrt to how we do this today? Definitely the controllers can't change the way they compute the hash function between versions (currently fnv). We can add support for that if we think that we will have a need to change the hash computation in the future. The controllers only track `Spec.Template` for the purposes of history, so the place where we aren't resilient is modifying the defaults in the PodTemplateSpec for the Workloads API resources, but I thought we had agreed that defaults that would apply to Pods should be added to the Pod resource and not workload API resources?

> Is there a particular problem that impacts the user wrt to how we do this today?

Yes, see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/95587#issuecomment-731497172

> API server upgrade triggers new rollout of a workload with no changes/writes to the workload object, due to a delta between the read object and the snapshotted controller revision. An example was the procMount defaulting which caused a daemonset or deployment to replace all its pods on API upgrade. (#78633)

I'd recommend taking the controller discussion back to there and keep this issue focused on the kubelet.
Just to be clear on the implications of this - we're blocking API changes that could trigger this, so the project overall is being impacted.

@liggitt I tend to think that all maintenance of the kubelet should warrant a drain (major/minor/patch).  I guess a cluster that is a single node is the potential outlier, need to reflect on that a little bit though.  @thockin what changes have we blocked?  I was not aware of the impact this was having across the project as the general concept of drain, update kubelet was basically the primary path I had seen everywhere for o(years).

caught up with @liggitt separately and now properly understand this.  the kubelet should hash on fields that it understands as mutable for the life of the container.  basically anything today that is editable in validate pod update.

To cut off the container spec field version mantenance effort, how about adding a container label hashVersion valued with the current kubelet version, if the hashVersion read from existent container is null or not matched with current kubelet version, just skip the change detection? The container would be recreated with new hash method by future pod updates. If any risks are concerned, kubelet should provide a configuration parameter switch to let user evaluate whether to turn it on or not during k8s upgrade.
@derekwaynecarr

> To cut off the container spec field version mantenance effort, how about adding a container label hashVersion valued with the current kubelet version, if the hashVersion read from existent container is null or not matched with current kubelet version, just skip the change detection?

The current issue is not related to the kubelet version, but changes to the API server version. I think the kubelet hashing on container fields it knows can change and expects to handle is the right approach (currently just image name, I think; in the future, container resources as well)
@liggitt i see, if any final decision or approach on progress now?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/63814#issuecomment-767775821 seems like agreement from sig-node representative:

> the kubelet should hash on fields that it understands as mutable for the life of the container. basically anything today that is editable in validate pod update.

But I don't see an assignee or any work in progress here. Marked this as needs-triage to bubble it up to the sig issue review process.
So under this pattern, if new API Container adds new mutable field with default value, the restart is unavoidable, right? @liggitt

this would have to be a container field that 1) the API server defaults, 2) the kubelet expects to be mutable and explicitly includes in its container hash

Because the kubelet has to be aware of the field, it would be reasonable for it to use the default value in the hash if the field was unpopulated.


https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/78914 added unit tests that will catch default changes to podspec and container
